reasoning: Dogfood cron 2026-08-05 05:5xZ: ~/.hermes/scripts/dogfood-pick.py failed with 'DOGFOOD PICKER: no enabled projects with workdirs' although the API returns 45 enabled projects with workdirs. title: 🟢 P2 — Daemon stuck in exec-fallback permanently when the Hermes gateway API (:8642) is down at startup: reconnector never re-engages HTTP + --no-exec-fallback ignored on the startup path. On 2026-08-14 the gateway died ~14:41 (no clean exit record; earlyoom prefers hermes/python processes and the gateway ran ~2GB RSS) and the 14:53:47 daemon restart found :8642 unreachable after 10/10 retries → fell back to exec.Command (spawns_exec=89 / spawns_http=0 since, vs 6/0 at tick #367). main.go's background reconnector has `if !gwConnected { continue }` — a daemon that STARTS in fallback mode never attempts reconnection, so even a healthy gateway later leaves the fleet spawning full `hermes chat -q` processes forever (until the next daemon restart). title: Session resume-after-restart: detect drops, find orphans, nudge them to continue
description: Bane 2026-09-01: when the gateway drops or restarts, in-flight sessions should be RESUMABLE, not lost. Design: (1) DROP DETECTION — gateway shutdown hook + scheduler heartbeat watcher mark in-flight sessions 'orphaned' with their last prompt/state; (2) ORPHAN SCAN — on gateway health-return, find sessions whose parent tick/session is still incomplete (works best for prompt-based sessions; dagger script sessions need the pipeline-level equivalent: DAGGER RESUME — the dagger run dir + node state survive an interruption, so a resumed run continues from the last completed node rather than from scratch); (3) THE NUDGE — re-queue the session with a continuation prompt that includes its last state ('you were doing X, last completed Y, continue') instead of restarting cold; (4) IDEMPOTENCE — a resumed session must not double-commit (guard already checks tree state). Build order: prompt-session nudge first (cheap, high value), dagger .d5s/node-state resume second. Pass criteria: kill the gateway mid-tick; on restart the tick's session is re-nudged and completes without manual intervention; no duplicate commits.

title: MCP write-tool coverage stops at weight/priority/cooldown/decay — model/provider/budget/prompt/enable changes force REST-or-SQL workarounds
description: Bane 2026-09-02 schema-vs-write-path sweep. The MCP registry (internal/mcp/server.go:64-196) exposes exactly four per-project write tools: fleet_set_weight, fleet_set_priority, fleet_set_cooldown, fleet_set_decay — plus fleet_add which accepts ONLY name/repo/repo_url/workdir/weight (internal/mcp/server.go:155-168). An MCP-only agent cannot: change a project's model/provider pair (the most common routing op in this fleet — fallback tier, worker tier, idle tier, no_global_fallback all unreachable), set daily/weekly/final budgets, set prompt/prompt_mode, enable/disable a project, or set deliver (SCHED-GAP-095 item 5 covers deliver). Every one of those is writable via REST PUT, so the workaround is 'know to drop to curl with the API key' — exactly the friction MCP exists to remove. FIX (minimal, no mega-tool): add fleet_set_model {name, model, provider} (one coherent pair per Bane doctrine), fleet_set_budget {name, daily?, weekly?, final?}, fleet_set_prompt {name, prompt, prompt_mode?}, fleet_set_enabled {name, enabled} (reuse GAP-044 provenance semantics from database.UpdateProject), and widen fleet_add's InputSchema with the optional fields the REST POST already takes (priority, cooldown_s, model, provider, namespace_id, deliver, budgets, prompt, prompt_mode). Handlers mirror toolFleetSetDecay (internal/mcp/handlers.go) calling database.UpdateProject. GUARD: MCP server_test.go cases per tool — happy path mutates the row, unknown project errors cleanly, fleet_add with model+namespace creates the row with them set.

title: Resume-on-unpaused wedges the eval loop (LOOP: paused) — proven 2026-09-06 fleet-wide 30-min stall
description: BUG: loop.go pause/resume share ONE channel (pauseCh chan bool). Pause() sends false, Resume() sends true, and the loop's select case <-l.pauseCh fires on ANY value: it logs 'LOOP: paused' then blocks in an inner select waiting for the NEXT pauseCh value. So POST /api/v1/resume on an UNPAUSED loop enters the pause branch and wedges forever (inner select never receives again; health ticker + GAP-042 stall watchdog are not active inside the inner select). PROVEN 2026-09-06: schedulerd-build.sh deploy (restart-when-drained.sh pattern) restarted the unit at 15:31:11, new daemon booted UNPAUSED and re-nudged orphans, then the deployer's final 'curl -X POST /api/v1/resume' at 15:31:20 wedged the fresh daemon into 'LOOP: paused'. Fleet sat with evaluation_age climbing (no ticks) 15:31:20->16:02:17 CT (~31 min) while /api/v1/status reported paused=null and the deployer believed scheduling was resumed (HTTP 200). Recovered by POSTing resume a SECOND time (inner select received true -> 'LOOP: resumed'). FIX: state-track pause (bool+mutex); Resume() no-ops when not paused, Pause() no-ops when already paused; or make the handler idempotent. SCHED-GAP-090's restart wrapper must NOT POST resume after a restart (fresh daemon boots unpaused) unless it first confirmed the daemon is paused. Also: GET /api/v1/status returns paused=null (not bool) — a pause-state endpoint/field is needed for safe automation.
reasoning: Supervisor 2026-09-06 16:02 CT recovery: journal showed 'LOOP: paused' 30s after unit restart with only duckbrain SYNC cycles since; restart-when-drained.sh (deployer, paused at 15:28:17, restart 15:31:11) POSTs resume as its final step -> channel asymmetry wedged the fresh daemon. Code: internal/scheduler/loop.go:335-343 + server.go:235-253. Single resume POST un-wedged it; evaluation_age 1783s -> 5s; ticks flowing. FIXED 2026-09-09 commit b4e52d0: pause state moved to an atomic flag (idempotent Pause/Resume), evaluate() gates on it, checkEvalStall returns early while paused, /api/v1/status now exposes 'paused'. Regression test: internal/scheduler/gap101_resume_wedge_test.go (kill-shot + pause-gating + post-resume recovery). title: SPEC+IMPL: task bump — temp speed-up (N ticks at floor cooldown, auto-revert) via API/UI, per-task and per-block
reasoning: BANE DIRECTIVE 2026-09-12 (the programmatic bankai): a task, a block of tasks, or a whole project can be given a quick bump — roughly 5 ticks running at a SMALL cooldown (7200 killer-lane floor is the natural bump cadence) — then AUTO-REVERTS. Not manual cooldown edits (today's boardctl 21600-to-7200 hand-PUT is the pattern to replace): the bump must be first-class, self-expiring, and correctly evaluated. SEMANTICS: (1) Bump targets: a task id, a block id (tasks sharing a block prefix or blocks-member set), or a project. (2) A bump = {target, ticks:N default 5, cooldown default 7200, reason REQUIRED}; SPEC MUST DECIDE: bump respects the 6h cooldown law floor (5 quick ticks = 5 consecutive eligible evals at 6h = too slow, so recommend bumps as the ONE sanctioned sub-6h lane with hard cap N<=8) — make the call explicit in the spec with rationale. (3) While active: packer treats project as bump-cooldown + boosted urgency (same class as the pending-work boost); normal adaptive tick-end evaluation CONTINUES so real work extends speed and idle burns bump ticks without extending anything. (4) AUTO-REVERT: after N ticks OR 12h hard-cap window, cooldown/floor/ceiling restore to pre-bump values; revert survives daemon restart (bump state persisted in DB: bump_remaining_ticks, bump_cooldown, bump_reason, bump_saved_cooldown/floor/ceiling columns) and survives fleet-cooldown-policy --apply regen (policy script reads active bumps and re-applies post-regen; fleet.toml itself NEVER carries bump keys). (5) SURFACES: POST /api/v1/projects/{name}/bump {task_id?|block_id?|project-wide, ticks, reason}; GET status shows bump badge + remaining count; dashboard button. (6) EVALUATION: ticks spawned during a bump carry bump=true (ticks table + delivered reports) so yield analysis can compare bump vs normal ticks. ACCEPTANCE: bump 5 -> next 5 eligible evals at bump cooldown -> 6th reverts to saved values; restart mid-bump -> survives with remaining count; policy regen --apply -> bump re-applied; idle project bumped -> 5 fast ticks, revert, no streak change; a tick completing real work during bump still earns normal adaptive progress; tests cover all of these.

title: SPEC: concurrent wave scheduling — scheduler-side support for one foreman running multi-worker waves in worktrees
reasoning: CONTEXT (skills now codify it: foreman 2.10.0 wave semantics + worker 1.6.0 sibling awareness; Bane architecture call 2026-09-12: ONE foreman per project dispatching WAVES of workers in git worktrees — NOT multiple foremen per workspace, board writers must serialize per SCHED-GAP-103). Scheduler-side questions the spec must answer so waves and the scheduler cooperate instead of fighting: (1) tick wall-clock: a 3-worker wave with guard+judge per branch can exceed the 2h tick-timeout — spec must decide per-namespace wave tick-timeout bump vs wave budget accounting vs timeout only counts FOREMAN-side merge phase (workers already ran). (2) cost/visibility: a wave tick spawns up to 3 workers = 3x model spend in one tick; ticks table should carry worker_count so cost reporting and the hop-rate ledger attribute waves correctly (today a wave looks like one tick one worker). (3) concurrency accounting: wave workers are OS processes INSIDE one tick — they must NOT consume scheduler slots (max_concurrent stays foreman-count), but the namespace cap should know a wave is running for load-shedding decisions (spec: expose wave_depth in status, decide whether namespace-cap counts waves). (4) bump interplay (SCHED-GAP-107): bump ticks N=5 with waves=3 means up to 15 worker runs — is that intended leverage or does bump cap waves to 1 worker? Spec decides with rationale. (5) failure shape: wave member fails judge -> rework loop inside the same tick (existing doctrine) vs next tick; a crashed foreman mid-wave must leave the in_progress marks + worktree list recoverable (skills already mark in_progress pre-dispatch; scheduler zombie-reaper should know worktrees exist). Acceptance: spec doc with decisions + rationale for all 5, then follow-up implementation rows.

title: Namespace wave_workers_cap + WAVE_BUDGET: advisory prompt injection at spawn, tick-boundary shed in packer_select.go
reasoning: S12 §6.2 (DECISION 3) + implementation row 5 of §16. wave_workers_cap (0 = unlimited) bounds concurrent WORKER processes per namespace across all its running ticks; it cannot be enforced inside a tick (workers are grandchildren), so it is enforced in two layers: (1) composition — the scheduler injects 'WAVE_BUDGET: <n>' into the foreman prompt where n = cap - live_wave_depth(namespace), 0 meaning 'serial tick, do not compose a wave this tick'; (2) admission — when cap>0 and the namespace has an in-flight tick with worker_count>0 not yet completed, packer_select.go does not select further projects in that namespace for a wave (it selects at most projects it can start with WAVE_BUDGET: 0). Invariant W1/W3: SlotPool and namespace max_concurrent still count TICKS only — one wave = one slot; no worker ever enters SlotPool.running/reserved/RunningSet()/active_ticks. Tests per §12 (TestNamespaceCap_CountsWaveTickAsOne + the slot-pool/RunningSet regressions) and the §12 integration step 7 (cap=3 with a live 3-wave -> next eval packs a serial tick). title: Dormant system-unit relic carries the LIVE gateway API_SERVER_KEY in a world-readable (0644) file — scrub + rotation decision
reasoning: Foreman-verified first-hand 2026-09-18 (tick 08-42-46), no secret material printed anywhere: /etc/systemd/system/coding-hermes-scheduler.service is mode 0644 (world-readable) and carries a literal Environment=API_SERVER_KEY=<43-char value>. title: Single time choke point + env-gated TEST TIME SIMULATOR: one wrapper function for all clock reads, with SCHEDULER_TIME_MODE=sim + scale (10x/100x/1000x) + skip-to-next-timer so evals run in seconds, not real hours
reasoning:
OWNER-REQUESTED (Bane, 2026-09-18): 'make sure it calls time via a wrapper function this way when tests are running you can have [an] env[ar] flag that you can use that puts it in test time simulator ... instead of running the test for a fixed period of real clock time the test knows how to do check in points like what time to skip the clock forward or just to run at a 10x or 100x or 1000x speed ... so that its not real clock time going but it allows the full eval fast'.

MEASURED at HEAD 2026-09-18 (grep over non-test internal/+cmd/): 87 direct time.Now() call sites (scheduler 53, dashboard 14, sync 6, api 5, database 3, blocks 3, cmd 2, mcp 1) PLUS 22 time.Since, 9 time.Sleep, 8 time.NewTicker, 7 time.After, 2 time.AfterFunc, 1 time.Until. Time is read from the wall clock in 139 places.

A NARROW SEAM ALREADY EXISTS and is the right seed, but does not do what was asked: Loop.nowFn (ADV-R04/G6, internal/scheduler/loop.go:37-42,177,215-234) is a single func() time.Time pinned by SetClock() and read via nowLocked() for evaluate()'s DECISION INSTANT only. It buys determinism (fixed instant -> exact set equality), NOT speed: nothing advances the clock, and every wait is still real. internal/scheduler/clock_seam_test.go pins it to a constant future instant precisely BECAUSE real time never moves in the test.

COST OF THE GAP, live: every test that exercises a wall-clock boundary must either sleep for real or assert nothing. The board already carries four flaky wall-clock casualties: CI-005 ('flaky wall-clock assertion in TestMigrateV27_WaveColumnsAndTickWork'), INT-CI-002 ('TestSchedGap066_ProjectsPayloadBudget is UTC-midnight-flaky'), SCHED-GAP-119 (activity deadline), and the drain/escalation paths that SCHED-GAP-143/145/146 just hardened - those tests can only run a few virtual minutes because minutes are what they cost in real time. An end-to-end 24h fleet simulation is currently impossible to run in CI.
detail:
ASK: exactly one wrapper for every clock read/wait in the daemon, plus an env-gated simulator behind it so a test or a whole-binary run can drive virtual time at 10x/100x/1000x or skip straight to the next armed timer.

1. NEW PACKAGE internal/clock - the ONLY place that may touch the stdlib time package for clock reads:
   type Clock interface {
     Now() time.Time
     Since(t time.Time) time.Duration
     Until(t time.Time) time.Duration
     Sleep(d time.Duration)
     After(d time.Duration) <-chan time.Time
     NewTicker(d time.Duration) *Ticker   // .C chan, .Stop()
     AfterFunc(d time.Duration, f func()) *Timer
   }
   clock.Real() -> stdlib delegation (production default, behaviour identical to today). clock.Sim() -> virtual clock.
   Injection is by CONSTRUCTOR (each package takes a Clock), never a package-level global - so two tests in one binary    can hold different clocks.

2. SIM CLOCK SEMANTICS - this is the 'check in points' part:
   - virtual now starts at SCHEDULER_TIME_START and does NOT advance on its own;
   - AdvanceBy(d) / AdvanceTo(t) move it deterministically and fire every timer whose deadline has passed, in (deadline, registration-sequence) order, so a schedule is reproducible run-to-run;
   - SCHEDULER_TIME_SCALE=<float> (default 1.0) is the 10x/100x/1000x speed: a blocked Sleep(d)/After(d) costs d/scale of REAL time (so Sleep(1h) at 1000x is 3.6s real); the virtual clock still reads 1h later, so production comparisons are unchanged;
   - SCHEDULER_TIME_AUTOADVANCE=1 is 'skip the clock forward': when no goroutine is runnable and >=1 timer is armed, jump virtual time to the earliest armed timer and fire it (event-driven, deterministic); with zero armed timers it is a no-op - no busy loop, no spin;
   - a test-only control surface (AdvanceBy/AdvanceTo/RunUntilIdle) on the Sim clock so Go tests drive it directly; the env vars are for whole-binary runs (e.g. --simulate, the smoke test).

3. ENV-FLAG CONTRACT:
   SCHEDULER_TIME_MODE      real (default) | sim
   SCHEDULER_TIME_SCALE     positive float, default 1.0
   SCHEDULER_TIME_START     RFC3339 instant (sim only)
   SCHEDULER_TIME_AUTOADVANCE  0|1, default 0
   Resolution order CLI flag < env < TOML, matching the budget chain (ADV-R09), with provenance surfaced like budget_source. FAIL CLOSED: sim mode is a fatal boot error unless explicitly requested (SCHEDULER_TIME_MODE=sim), and it must refuse to run against a configured --gateway-url unless --simulate is also set - a stray env var must never silently put the production daemon on a fake clock.

4. MIGRATION: route all 139 call sites through the seam (87 Now + 22 Since + 9 Sleep + 8 Ticker + 7 After + 2 AfterFunc + 1 Until). Loop.nowFn (ADV-R04) is REPLACED by the injected Clock - the existing seam tests must stay green, unchanged in intent. Pure helpers (time.Parse, time.Duration, time.Date construction) are NOT clock reads and stay direct.

5. THE GUARD (load-bearing, mirrors ADV-R10's no-second-ceiling test): TestNoDirectStdlibTimeOutsideClock statically scans non-test sources under internal/ and cmd/ and FAILS if time.Now()/time.Since(/time.Until(/time.Sleep(/time.After(/time.NewTicker(/time.AfterFunc( appears anywhere other than internal/clock. The allowlist starts EMPTY. Without this guard the seam rots the first time a new codepath reaches for time.Now().

ACCEPTANCE TESTS:
  AC1 guard test above, RED-proven: add one time.Now() to an unrelated file -> guard fails; remove -> passes.
  AC2 SCHEDULER_TIME_MODE unset/real: existing suite green, zero behaviour change (default path is pure stdlib delegation).
  AC3 cooldown expiry: project with cooldown 3600s is NOT selected at T0, IS selected after one AdvanceBy(3601s), asserted with a REAL wall-clock stopwatch under 200ms.
  AC4 escalation: floor 900 + no_progress_threshold 10 driven to the derived ceiling (8x floor) in exact tick order in under 1s real.
  AC5 armed timers: the 30s health ticker and the 60s board-wake poller fire at exact virtual instants (e.g. board write -> wake at +5m virtual) via AUTOADVANCE, with no real wait.
  AC6 PAYOFF - whole-daemon E2E: boot the binary in sim mode against a fixture, run ~24h of virtual time, and show the fleet complete N ticks plus a full drain-restart cycle in under 10s real. This is the deliverable the request is for.
  AC7 fail-closed: SCHEDULER_TIME_MODE=sim with a real --gateway-url and no --simulate exits non-zero with an explicit message.

SLICING (the row is deliberately splittable across ticks - land in this order):
  P1a internal/clock package + interface + Real + Sim + its own unit tests (timer ordering, AutoAdvance, scale, no-spin).
  P1b the guard test + route internal/scheduler (53 Now + the hot waits: cooldown, tick timeout, drain deadline, escalation window, board-wake debounce, spawn lease).
  P1c E2E sim harness + convert the wall-clock-flaky tests (CI-005, INT-CI-002, SCHED-GAP-119) to the simulator.
  P2  remaining packages: dashboard, sync, api, database, blocks, mcp, cmd.

DO NOT: introduce a package-level global clock, change production timing semantics, or make sim reachable without an explicit opt-in. Production behaviour at SCHEDULER_TIME_MODE=real must be provably identical to today (AC2 is the proof).

title: Gateway-unreachable is 89% of ALL tick failures (795 of 892 in 7 days) — gate spawns on gateway health instead of charging every lane
reasoning: Measured 2026-09-11..09-18 from scheduler.db: 2,469 ticks, 892 failed/timeout, and 795 of those (89%) carry one error: 'gateway unreachable and exec fallback disabled: gateway POST'. Worst day 09-16: 937 ticks, 723 failed (77%) — the scheduler kept packing and spawning into a dead gateway, so each failed spawn was written as a lane fault (2 per lane across ~20 lanes), consumed a slot, a packer pick and a cooldown cycle. 09-18 03:39-03:41 alone contributed 43 on a single gateway restart, and the residual daily rate is ~13% (48/day), almost all transport. The tick runs with --no-exec-fallback by policy, so an unreachable gateway is a hard failure instead of a retry. Acceptance: a regression test asserting a spawn against a down gateway leaves the row queued and writes no failure; and a 7-day rerun where the gateway-unreachable share is a small fraction of failures.

title: POOL half of SCHED-GAP-146: SlotPool.spawn defers a load-gated spawn AFTER the row is enqueued → the row strands 'queued' forever (nothing dispatches an existing row)
reasoning: The nudge half of 146 is fixed (resumeOrphans now consults LoadGateShouldDefer before bumping the nudge count) but the POOL half remains and is the general case. First-hand code + log evidence 2026-09-18: internal/scheduler/slot_pool.go:297-316 — when LoadGateShouldDefer(db, proj.NamespaceID) is true the branch logs 'LOAD-GATE: deferring <proj> (tick <id>) — load N >= threshold T (work stays queued)' and RETURNS, leaving the row the CALLER already enqueued sitting in status='queued'. Nothing in the daemon dispatches an existing row: the packer picks a project and calls spawn again (which re-consults the gate and can strand another row), SpawnNow 409s the project, and the orphan scan treats the stranded row as in-flight — so the work is neither running nor eligible. Live proof: 5 rows sitting queued >1h right now while load is 14-20, plus the 7 zombies reconciled by hand this morning (SCHED-GAP-145 class) — both are this branch. Fix direction, in order of preference: (a) consult the gate BEFORE the row is created (make the enqueue conditional so a deferral never produces a queued row), or (b) on deferral mark the row with a deferred_reason + a re-check trigger on gate-open, so 'defer-not-drop' means a queued row that something actually re-drives. Either way it must stay defer-not-drop: no cooldown consumed, no failure recorded, nudge budget untouched. Acceptance: a regression test asserting that after a gate deferral the row is EITHER absent (b: re-driven) and the project is picked again on the next evaluation with the gate open, and that a repeated deferral never accumulates queued rows; plus a live check that the queued-row count returns to 0 after the load falls.

title: 32% of all ticks (836/week, ~$2,030 sticker) come from non-code lanes whose output is recorded NOWHERE — the QA family records exactly zero
reasoning: Measured 2026-09-12..19 across all 90 enabled lanes: the primary foremen (26 lanes) do 1,747 ticks -> 1,668 code commits + 829 board commits for $19,535 sticker. Two readings and the data cannot currently tell them apart: (a) these lanes do real work whose output our columns do not capture (sync writes DuckBrain keys, pm files rows, dogfood reports findings, qa audits) — in which case the metric is blind, not the lanes; or (b) they are idle-spinning on empty or unactionable input. Evidence favouring (a) is real: PM ticks DO commit board rows to git (many 'board: PM tick ...' commits exist) yet board_commits reads 0 for them, and sync lanes have no board file at <workdir>/.coding-hermes/board/tasks.jsonl to count. Requirement: give every non-code family a recorded output metric — qa: findings filed (rows with qa provenance), pm: rows filed, sync: DuckBrain keys written + verified, dogfood: findings filed — persist it on the tick row, surface it in /api/v1/status and the fleet board, and only THEN judge cadence. Acceptance: every enabled lane shows a non-null output count for its family on the board; a lane with zero recorded output across >=8 consecutive ticks raises a HIGH event naming it.

Findings, first-hand from the live DB 2026-09-19: (a) heading is DISABLED with disabled_at 2026-08-02T10:46:39Z / disabled_by 'legacy' — and heading-qa, heading-pm, heading-sync, heading-dogfood have been ENABLED ever since, i.e. four sister lanes reading a parked project's board (which still carried 13 pending rows) for seven weeks; (b) the same shape appeared twice inside one hour today: a PM lane paused coding-hermes-tools (13:09:43Z) and concurrently a sibling plus-ultra release paused trouble (13:21:29Z, reason 'plus-ultra wave: foreman lane paused during concurrent-worktree'), and in both cases the satellites stayed enabled until the invariant gate named them. WHY IT MATTERS: satellites read the primary's board through a symlink, so an enabled satellite on a parked target keeps consuming namespace cap-1 slots and burning ticks on work whose owner is off; the tick budget is the fleet's scarcest resource (see the yield work). Requirement: pausing (or disabling) a project cascades to its -qa/-pm/-sync/-dogfood lanes (stamp them with the same provenance + a 'paused by target' marker), and restoring the target restores exactly those lanes it parked — never a lane parked by an operator for its own reasons. Acceptance: a regression test that pauses a primary and asserts all four satellites report disabled with provenance naming the target, and a restore that re-enables exactly those four; plus the invariant check stays green through a pause/restore cycle.

title: Board-vocab gate vs foreman wave: the wave writes status=in_progress into tasks.jsonl while the CI gate rejects that spelling, so any board commit composed after a wave dispatch ships off-vocabulary rows and turns main red (caught on run 35503463963)

title: [P1] /api/v1/status takes 18-30s (and /api/v1/projects spikes >18s) — it times out the fleet-cooldown-policy, which then silently fails to regenerate fleet.toml
reasoning: FOUND WHILE RUNNING THE OPS SCRIPT, and it BLOCKS it. `fleet-cooldown-policy.py` (the only writer of fleet.toml) calls /api/v1/projects with a hardcoded urllib timeout of 10s. Measured 2026-09-21 12:56 on a quiet-ish fleet: /api/v1/status = 18.63s on one call and TIMEOUT at 30s on the next; /api/v1/projects = 18.76s on one call but 0.23/0.27/0.24s on the three immediately after. So there are at least two distinct problems and only one of them is obvious: (a) /api/v1/status is CONSISTENTLY slow (18-30s+, unusable for any poller), and (b) /api/v1/projects has a high-variance tail - fast when the fleet is calm, >18s under load (loadavg was 21.27 during the slow sample, above the 12 load gate). The policy timed out twice in a row on (b) and could not regenerate fleet.toml at all - meaning a scheduler RESTART during that window would have reloaded STALE pins from the previous fleet.toml. That is the real risk: the durable store silently stops tracking reality whenever the API is slow, and nothing reports it. WHY IT MATTERS BEYOND THE SCRIPT: /api/v1/status is the dashboard's and every monitoring poller's primary read, and the per-project failure-rate breakdown it carries was added over a --failure-window of 100 ticks per project - with 368 project rows that is a plausible O(projects x window) path, so the suspect is the failure-rate computation and/or a missing index on ticks(project_name, spawned_at). Reproduce: time the calls back to back - `for i in 1 2 3; do curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{time_total}\n' http://127.0.0.1:9090/api/v1/status; done` and the same for /api/v1/projects while a wave is running. Acceptance: /api/v1/status returns in well under 1s warm on the live fleet (368 projects, 73k ticks) with its numbers unchanged, /api/v1/projects has no >2s tail under load, and fleet-cooldown-policy.py --apply completes inside its 10s per-request budget. NOTE the shape of this bug: it was invisible for as long as nothing polled the endpoint on a timer. A slow endpoint is not a cosmetic defect when a script's correctness depends on it.

The deployed .hermes/scripts/fleet-cooldown-policy.py had been OVERWRITTEN in place on 2026-09-21 18:45:59 with a variant that matches NO committed revision (23968 bytes vs HEAD's 29904) - HEAD minus Bane's 2026-09-19 rulings and minus the --verify tripwire. Lost from the deployed copy: ELEVATED_PINS entries 'hermes-dagger': 900 (Bane 2026-09-15 15min ruling), 'hermes-canopy': 21600 (Bane 2026-09-17 all coding-hermes primaries at 21600), 'hermes-canopy-releng': 86400 (Bane 2026-09-19 releng is 24h not 6h); OPERATOR_7200 was re-populated with dagger/canopy at 7200 (HEAD has it EMPTY, emptied 2026-09-19 for exactly this reason); and the SCHED-GAP-121/181 --verify pin tripwire plus its usage doc and the TASKS-ADMISSION LAW comment were deleted. CONSEQUENCE - three of Bane's rulings were being silently violated in the durable store and nothing reported it: the regen wrote 7200 for dagger and canopy, so the next scheduler restart would have snapped both back to 2h, and canopy-releng to 6h instead of 24h. THE FALSE GREEN is the important half: because the deployed copy had no --verify handling at all, `fleet-cooldown-policy.py --verify` fell through to the dry-run path, printed a normal table and EXITED 0 - the safety net for pin drift was answering green while every pin it exists to police was wrong. title: [P1] satellite lanes reuse a row id as a recurring SLOT and never close the previous row - 29% of open rows fleet-wide collide on id and 95 slots have never closed one
reasoning: THE ROOT CAUSE of the fleet's board inflation, and nothing owns it today. The satellite lanes (-qa/-dogfood/-pm/-sync and the dagger-driven QA/DF generators) reuse a FIXED row id as a recurring SLOT and append each cycle's new finding under it WITHOUT closing the previous row. Measured 2026-09-22 across 53 boards: 2,352 open rows, of which 683 (29%) are id-collisions with another open row on the SAME board; 106 slots hold 3+ open rows under one id (730 rows); 95 of those slots have NEVER closed a single row (670 rows). Worst: QA-CONSENSUS-1 = 85 open rows under one id, QA-HIVEMIND-WORK-1 = 39. WHY IT SURVIVES: (a) exact-content fingerprint dedupe reports only 3.9% duplication, because each cycle RE-WORDS the same condition and mints a fresh hash - so every existing dedupe tool reports a clean board while the id is saturated; (b) no lane is responsible for closing another lane's row; (c) the rows frequently describe artifacts in OTHER repos (bunker host faults, ~/.hermes/scripts harness bugs), so the project foreman cannot close them even when the fix has landed - consensus re-filed one port-pool fault 47 times under 40 titles AFTER the fix shipped in bunker-qa.sh. CONSEQUENCE: 'open rows' is not a work count, it is a work count plus an unbounded log, and every derived metric (burndown charts, 'is this project done') inherits the error. WHAT I ALREADY DID (not a substitute): a safe pass flagged 48 never-completable fixture rows perpetual:true and closed 24 exact duplicates. WHAT THIS ROW ASKS FOR, in order: (1) unique ids - the satellite must mint a unique id per FILED FINDING, never reuse one as a slot (this is the 'naming' fix and it must land at the generator, not by rewriting boards); (2) a close-on-refile rule - when a lane re-diagnoses a condition it already has an open row for, it must annotate or close the old row in the same commit rather than appending a sibling; (3) condition-level dedupe as a PM-lane job (the existing doctrine says dedupe by CONTENT fingerprint and annotate with superseded_by) - the ~683 id-collision rows were deliberately NOT mass-closed because deciding 'same finding re-worded' vs 'distinct claim sharing a slot' is judgement, and closing a distinct claim destroys real work. Acceptance: a fresh board-commit cycle adds zero id-collisions and closes as many rows as it files; re-running the audit shows the 29% collision rate falling and the 95 zero-terminal slots shrinking. title: [P2] Ops watchdog's authoritative unit-state signal is inert in production: the system watchdog.timer has no user bus, so 'systemctl --user is-active coding-hermes-scheduler' returns empty and UNIT_ACTIVE=unknown on EVERY run — the 2026-09-21 'consult the systemd unit FIRST' branch can never fire (observed 2026-09-22 15:14:30: ambiguity branch + exit 0 while the unit WAS active and the daemon WAS up)
reasoning:
Filed by the SCHED-GAP-204-210 deploy worker (2026-09-22) while measuring the watchdog for SCHED-GAP-204.

EVIDENCE (live, not read from source):
`journalctl -u watchdog.service` at 15:14:30 printed:
  "⚠️ Scheduler probes failing (live=unsupported health=000) while the systemd unit state is UNDETERMINABLE in this context — cannot prove an outage. Verify: systemctl --user status coding-hermes-scheduler"
and the unit then deactivated "successfully" (exit 0). Tracing the same run in the audit log shows the watchdog's own commands executing with cwd=/ under the system-scope timer: `systemctl --user is-active coding-hermes-scheduler` from that context produces EMPTY output (no XDG_RUNTIME_DIR / session bus), so `UNIT_ACTIVE` is set to `unknown` on every production run.

WHY IT MATTERS: watchdog.sh's 2026-09-21 hardening states "the verdict now consults the systemd unit FIRST (cheap, DB-free and authoritative) — a timed-out HTTP probe while the unit is active is reported as a slow-probe DEGRADED after 2 misses, never as DOWN". That authoritative branch can never execute in production because the unit state is always undeterminable there. The run instead takes the ambiguity branch (exit 0, writes a SLOW line). Consequence: no false DOWN (good, and the 09-22 hardening fixed that), but ALSO no DOWN detection through the unit signal — the strongest signal the design claims to rely on is inert. This is the "verify guards are ARMED, not merely present" defect class (SCHED-GAP-170 shape): present, unit-tested, merged, never executed.

SECOND ORDERING EFFECT: the streak file can only be reset by the "provably up" path, which requires `/api/v1/live` = 200. While the deployed build answered 404 there, the file grew unchecked — 31 SLOW lines by 15:14 (vs the 33 FAIL lines the 09-22 comment describes before the fix). So the watchdog's alert streak is currently a function of the DEPLOY gap, not of daemon health; the deploy in SCHED-GAP-210 clears it.

FIX DIRECTION (for the foreman, not applied here — this row exists so it is not lost): make the unit-state signal resolvable from the watchdog's own execution context, e.g. probe the unit by cgroup membership / `systemctl --user --machine=kara@.host is-active ...` with the runtime dir exported, or read `/run/user/1000/systemd` + the unit's cgroup (`/sys/fs/cgroup/.../coding-hermes-scheduler.service`) rather than relying on a session bus that the timer does not have; and/or have the timer run inside the user manager so `--user` works. Acceptance: a run that prints the unit-active branch (not the ambiguity branch) while the daemon is up. Do NOT "fix" it by removing the ambiguity branch — that branch is what prevents the false CRITICAL, and it should stay for genuinely undeterminable contexts.

RELATED: SCHED-GAP-204 (the /api/v1/live route + probe-budget split), SCHED-GAP-210 (the deploy gap that keeps /live 404 in the deployed build).

title: [P1] The 90-min CleanupStale backstop is SHORTER than the configured tick deadline, so legitimate long ticks are recorded as timeouts at exactly 90m
reasoning:
MEASURED 2026-09-22 by the supervisor tick, read-only over scheduler.db + source.

THE CONTRADICTION. internal/scheduler/tick_process.go:68 calls
  l.lifecycle.CleanupStaleProjects(90 * time.Minute)
with the duration HARDCODED. The real per-tick deadline is namespace-aware and strictly larger:
  - /api/v1/config tick_timeout = 2h0m0s (flag default)
  - namespaces row coding-hermes: wave_enabled=1, wave_tick_timeout=3h
  - spawn.go:1193 builds the tick ctx with context.WithTimeout(..., effectiveTimeout), where
    effectiveTimeout = env > namespace wave_tick_timeout > --tick-timeout (SCHED-GAP-111, ceiling 4h)
So for the 20 coding-hermes lanes the effective budget is 3h, yet any running tick older than 90m is
flipped to status=timeout by the per-eval reaper — a backstop that fires 2x EARLIER than the deadline
it is supposed to backstop. The code comment calls it the "self-heal backstop for any wedge a missed
reaper leaves behind", i.e. it is meant to be LAST, not first.

PROOF (today, same afternoon, same machine):
  auger        spawned 13:24:09 -> status=timeout 14:59:19, error="stale - timeout at 1h30m0s" (95m)
  hermes-dagger spawned 13:24:15 -> status=timeout 14:59:19, error="stale - timeout at 1h30m0s" (95m)
  heading      spawned 14:11:46 -> status=completed 15:46:27 (95m)
  terminal-jail spawned 13:37:20 -> status=completed 15:21:48 (104m)
heading and terminal-jail survived only because the loop was PAUSED from 15:14:17 (sanctioned
deploy drain), so evaluate() never ran and the 90m reaper never fired. The two that were reaped
crossed 90m while the loop was live. Note the timestamps: both reaps land on the SAME second
(14:59:19) because it is one evaluate() pass.

WHY IT MATTERS. These phantom timeouts are indistinguishable from real ones in every consumer:
  - ticks.status / failure-rate counters feed auto_disable (--auto-disable-failure-rate 0.9 over a
    100-tick window): a lane whose work legitimately takes 90-180m accumulates timeouts it never caused;
  - the 24h fleet census reads "100 failed + 6 timeout" of which auger/hermes-dagger here are not failures;
  - foremen/reviews reading the board see a timeout row for work that was still running.
Also observed 2026-09-22 14:59 in the same pass: it is the only reaper that fires while the loop is
paused-dead (CleanupStale lives inside evaluate()), so the wedge self-heal is unavailable exactly when
a deploy drain is waiting on the same long ticks.

ACCEPTANCE.
1. The reaper's maxAge is DERIVED from the effective deadline (namespace wave_tick_timeout >>
   --tick-timeout), with a documented grace margin, so it can never precede the deadline it backs up.
   If a fixed value is kept, it must be >= the 4h ceiling, not 90m.
2. A unit test asserts a running tick younger than its namespace's effective deadline is NOT flipped
   terminal by the cleanup path (regression guard, table-driven over ns inherit / 2h / 3h).
3. Evidence required in the report: a tick that legitimately exceeds 90m is allowed to reach its own
   deadline or complete, and its DB row shows completed/timeout from the spawn path, never
   error="stale - timeout at 1h30m0s".
4. State the paused-loop consequence explicitly: either move the backstop off the evaluate() path
   (so a drain can still self-heal a wedge) or document that a paused loop intentionally suspends it.
foreman_note:
DRAIN-WINDOW COROLLARY (measured 2026-09-22 16:05 while the deploy was in flight, read-only).

The same deadline disagreement bites the deploy path. scheduler-deploy-drain-restart.sh pauses
the loop, then polls active_ticks=0 for at most 480 x 15s = 120 min before giving up
("DRAIN TIMEOUT ... NOT restarting"), then resumes and exits 2. The 4 ticks it was waiting on were
all wave-enabled coding-hermes lanes, whose effective deadline is the NAMESPACE wave_tick_timeout
= 3h (not the 2h flag), so their ctx expiry is LATER than the drain deadline:

  tick spawned                 ctx expiry (+3h)      drain deadline
  trouble        14:21:56  ->  17:21:56          \
  bunker         14:34:42  ->  17:34:42           >  15:14:17 + 120m = 17:14:17
  warpfs         14:43:26  ->  17:43:26          /
  hermes-dagger  15:07:55  ->  18:07:55

Net effect: a deploy started while a wave tick is already ~1h old CANNOT drain, because the pause
that makes the restart safe is also what disables CleanupStale (it lives inside evaluate()). That is
the chicken-and-egg: the safety pause removes the only wedge reaper, so the drain has nothing to
rely on except the ticks finishing on their own, and the window is shorter than their legal budget.
The script's own header records the failure mode this creates ("the previous run died mid-drain and
left the fleet paused"), and it is why this tick left the loop paused rather than resuming it by hand.

FIX DIRECTION (fold into acceptance above, same root cause): the drain window must be >= the MAX
effective deadline in flight (env > namespace wave_tick_timeout > --tick-timeout, ceiling 4h), or the
reaper must be reachable while paused. A fixed 120-min window is strictly smaller than the 3h budget
it is waiting for, so the timeout is deterministic, not a race.

title: [P2] Wave verdicts are silently discarded: normalizeWaveJudge/normalizeWaveMerge are case-sensitive exact-match switches, so manifests writing "PASS <sha>" / "already merged as <sha>" store unknown/pending and leave 81 completed ticks with worker rows still state=running
reasoning:
MEASURED 2026-09-22 by the supervisor tick, read-only over scheduler.db + source + one live manifest.

THE INVARIANT THAT BREAKS. A completed tick must not leave its worker rows live. Measured now:
  132 tick_workers rows carry state='running'
   81 of them belong to ticks that are ALREADY status='completed' and older than 24h
So every reader that asks "which wave workers are actually running" gets a number that includes
81 finished waves' worth of rows.

CANONICAL INSTANCE (fully traced, not inferred).
  tick   crier-2026-09-19-19-37-43   ticks.status=completed   ticks.worker_count=7
  manifest  /home/kara/crier/.coding-hermes/waves/crier-2026-09-19-19-37-43.json exists, 7 workers,
            each carrying a real verdict and a real merge:
              DF-CRIER-274  judge="PASS 94b82015"  merge="already merged as 4ceb0c5"
              DF-CRIER-275  judge="PASS 505246b2"  merge="already merged as 40fdaca"
              DF-CRIER-264  judge="PASS ec2ca948"  merge="already merged as d64fe81"
              ... (7/7 the same shape)
  DB rows   all 7 read  judge='unknown'  merge='pending'  state='running'  commit_sha=''
The manifest's evidence is intact; the DB's copy of it is empty.

ROOT CAUSE (proven by reading the parser, no guessing). Both normalizers are case-sensitive
EXACT-MATCH switches:
  wave_manifest.go:91  normalizeWaveJudge(v): only the literal strings "pass" | "fail" | "withdrawn"
                       survive; default -> "unknown"
  wave_manifest.go:103 normalizeWaveMerge(v): only "merged" | "conflict" | "preserved";
                       default -> "pending"
and waveWorkerTerminalState (wave_manifest.go:177) returns 'running' precisely when BOTH are the
defaults. So the producer's vocabulary and the consumer's vocabulary disagree: manifests in the
wild write a human-readable verdict form ("PASS <sha>", "already merged as <sha>") while the parser
accepts only a bare lowercase token. Every such worker is stored unknown/pending/running.

WHY IT MATTERS.
  - Per-worker judge/merge/commit attribution (SCHED-GAP-115's per-task rollup) is unreadable from
    the DB: a PASS and a FAIL land in the same 'unknown' bucket.
  - The manifest is the ONLY correct source, but SCHED-GAP-110 moved worker attribution INTO the DB,
    so consumers were pointed at the lossy copy.
  - It degrades SILENTLY: no event is emitted when normalization discards a value (waveWarnEvent is
    used for manifest parse problems, not for vocabulary fallbacks), so a drift in the writer's
    output shape cannot be noticed from the daemon's logs.
  - 81 completed ticks currently make state-based queries wrong.

ACCEPTANCE.
1. normalizeWaveJudge/normalizeWaveMerge accept the shapes the manifests actually carry:
   case-insensitive, a leading verdict token with optional trailing evidence
   ("PASS 94b82015" -> pass, "FAIL <sha>" -> fail, "already merged as 4ceb0c5" -> merged,
   "conflict ..." -> conflict, "preserved ..." -> preserved, "withdrawn ..." -> withdrawn).
   Anything still unrecognized keeps degrading to unknown/pending, AND emits one WARN/MEDIUM event
   naming the raw value — a vocabulary mismatch must be visible, never silent.
2. Table-driven test using the VERBATIM strings from crier-2026-09-19-19-37-43.json, asserted to
   normalize to judge=pass / merge=merged.

THE DAEMON'S OWN WARNINGS: 'WARN: goroutine count = 1046 (threshold: 100)' - ~10x its own warning threshold, consistent with handlers piling up on a dependency that never returns (a request with no deadline); and 'BOARD-WAKE-WATCHDOG: poll loop silent for 5m0s (threshold 5m0s) - board-driven wake dead, clock cadence unaffected'. title: P1 — the fleet admitted no ticks for 6h45m on 09-23 (14:25-21:10 UTC) while the daemon was alive and evaluating: load1 hit 65.13 against a gate of 12, and 53% of samples were over it
foreman_note:
Filed by the review programme (D8) after Bane asked why the fleet went dark 14:00-20:53 (his window is UTC; 09:25:58-16:10:45 local).

WHAT DID NOT HAPPEN — checked, because the first hypothesis was wrong on both counts:
- **Nothing took the port.** `scheduler.log` shows `HTTP: listening on 127.0.0.1:9090` at 16:09:21 and again at 16:47:24 — first try, no bind error anywhere in the window. The 14 `listening on 127.0.0.1:9199` instances are the repo's OWN integration test (`integration_test.go:19 const testPort = ":9199"`, and CI runs `./bin/schedulerd -listen 127.0.0.1:9199 -db /tmp/sim-ci.db -sim-setup`); the `max_concurrent=10` in those lines is the test's default, not the fleet's.
- **The daemon was never down during the dark window.** It evaluated every pass; the events table is a continuous run of `load_gate deferred <lane>` entries from 13:30 through 16:05.
- The reboot was clean: `PrepareForShutdown` at 16:05:53 from the desktop session, boot at 16:07:19, daemon back at 16:09:21 — two minutes.

WHAT ACTUALLY HAPPENED: the load gate never opened. Its own telemetry (`scheduler.db:host_samples`, 358 samples in the window) shows load1 going 8-13 through midday, then 21.4 (13:14), 24.9 (13:41), 49.16 (14:41), 49.8 (15:19), 49.6 (15:49) — **peak 65.13 at 15:47:46** — with **189 of 358 samples (53%) at or above the threshold of 12**. The gate therefore deferred every lane for 6h45m: last tick 09:25:58 local, next 16:10:45. The gate is working as designed; it is doing what it was built to do on a box that is out of I/O.

ROOT CAUSE: processes in D state (uninterruptible I/O wait) — confirmed, and still true as I write: **18 processes in D right now** with **iowait 56%** and loadavg 54.8, dominated by **8x `cc1plus`** and a `dagger.test` binary, plus the kernel-side `jbd2/nvme0n1p2-8`, `ext4-rsv-conversion` kworker and compilers parked in `rq_qos_wait` (the block-layer QoS wait, i.e. the I/O scheduler throttling them). That signature is a LOCAL CGO compile/test storm against a single NVMe. It is the same shape as the 09-23 window, and it is why the box reads as "busy" when the useful fleet work is stalled: the fleet's own CPUs are idle while the storage layer is the bottleneck.

SECOND LOSS, SAME CLASS: at 16:47:23 the daemon logged `LOOP: shutdown drain timed out after 15s — marking in-flight ticks failed` and marked ten ticks failed (logsey, auger, digest, 9router, pulse, my-project, task-router-qa, hermes-dagger, auger-qa). title: [P1] Weight budget enforcement: make an over-budget namespace/lane actually HOLD work, not silently rescale
reasoning:
Operator ask 2026-09-24: "make sure the guard is correctly working so if we hit the budget of a namespace the server or a lane etc it will actaully pause things for us". MEASURED 2026-09-24 (live: ~/.hermes/coding-hermes/scheduler.db + the tree at HEAD). The panel in question: internal/dashboard/generator.go:531 and :536-539 render
Budget Used
{{.BudgetUsed}}/{{.BudgetTotal}}
Weight Budget{{.BudgetUsed}}/{{.BudgetTotal}}
The two operands are NOT the same kind of quantity: - BudgetUsed is the fleet-wide sum of EVERY enabled project's weight (internal/dashboard/generator_data.go:325 `data.BudgetUsed += r.Weight`). Live: 1218 (enabled) / 2109 (all rows) across 485 projects. - BudgetTotal is the PER-TICK packing budget (default 100; the daemon runs without --budget, so the documented default applies — generator_data.go:256-259). The packer spends that budget once per cycle (internal/scheduler/packer.go:274, "Greedy pack: pick projects that fit in budget"), so a fleet-wide sum can never sit under a per-tick budget: the panel is guaranteed to read "over budget" forever, and the ratio grows as the fleet grows. The fill is unclamped: internal/dashboard/generator_templates.go:35-40 "percent": func(used, total int) int { if total == 0 { return 0 }; return used * 100 / total } percent(1218, 100) == 1218, so the render is width:1218% — that is the bar running past the card edge, proven in source rather than guessed. Enforcement, measured: - The ONLY budget gate wired into the packer is SCHED-GAP-066, and it is USD SPEND, not weight: internal/scheduler/packer.go:86-89 SetBudgetGate, :189-191 calls it per project, and :63 documents the nil case as "no budget enforcement (tests, spend-query failure fail-open)" — i.e. the existing gate FAILS OPEN. - The weight budget has NO skip reason in the live code. specs/S04-weight-packer.md §3-4 defines SkipBudgetExhausted = "budget_exhausted" and a decision tree that skips a project when weight > budget_remaining, but grep for SkipBudgetExhausted / budget_exhausted / BudgetExhausted across internal/ returns ZERO hits. Spec and code have diverged. - What actually happens when asks exceed budget: internal/scheduler/namespace_alloc.go:58-66 if rTotal > budget { log.Printf("WARN NamespaceAllocator: total reserved %d exceeds budget %d; scaling reserved proportionally", ...) scale := float64(budget) / float64(rTotal) reserved[i] = math.Floor(float64(ns.Reserved) * scale) } So the fleet does not pause and does not refuse — it SILENTLY SHRINKS every namespace's reservation, and the only trace is a WARN in the daemon log. - Live oversubscription: 17 namespaces, sum(weight) = 248 against the same global budget of 100 (max single namespace = 100, the coding-hermes ns), so the fleet is ALREADY ~2.48x oversubscribed and every namespace is running at ~40% of its ask right now. - The real admission ceiling in practice is --max-concurrent 12 (fleet.toml-pinned, confirmed in the live daemon argv), with the load gate at 25. - No budget-exemption concept exists anywhere in the tree. Authority to extend, not replace: AGENTS.md lists "Budget authority chain (ADV-R09/G8)" among the standing design decisions, and internal/scheduler/advr09_budget_test.go + wave_budget.go own that chain. Any redefinition has to move through ADV-R09, not around it. The exemption convention to copy is SCHED-GAP-125 (namespace load-gate opt-out, load_gate='off', internal/config/config.go:319). THE FINDING: there is no weight-budget guard to make correct — the weight budget is ADVISORY today. Exceeding it does not pause, deny or hold anything; it proportionally shrinks every namespace reservation and logs one WARN. Any operator belief that "over budget == the fleet stops" is currently false. That is the defect this row fixes. SCOPE (decide, in writing, before building): (a) what the enforcement ACTION is at each level — namespace over its allocation, lane/project over its share, and the global budget as a whole. Options span deny-this-spawn / pause-the-namespace / hold-and-requeue; name which, per level. (b) what "pause" means operationally here, given admission_mode already has a `cooldown` and a `tasks` mode and namespaces carry load_gate. A pause must not become a second, competing admission mechanism — say how it composes. (c) whether the existing SCHED-GAP-066 spend gate and this weight gate are one gate or two, and whether the weight gate keeps the current fail-open nil behaviour (packer.go:63). Fail-open on a RESOURCE guard is a deliberate choice worth stating explicitly, not inheriting by default. (d) how this interacts with ADV-R09 (Budget authority chain) — extend that decision, do not fork it. (e) the reason must be OBSERVABLE: today the only evidence is a daemon-log WARN. Decide the tick skip-reason / event / API field that makes an over-budget hold visible to an operator and to the dashboard. BUILD / ACCEPTANCE: 1. A test that PROVES the gate fires: a namespace over its allocation produces the documented hold (no spawn) plus the recorded reason, and the reason is readable back. One negative arm proves it does NOT fire when under allocation. 2. No silent path: if work is held, something queryable says so. The namespace_alloc.go:58-66 proportional rescale either becomes the documented under-budget behaviour or is replaced — it must not survive as an undocumented side effect of an over-budget condition. 3. Behaviour under the live numbers is re-derived at merge time, not taken from this row (17 namespaces / 248 vs 100 today) — per the fleet's law that pre-run facts are re-derived rather than trusted. 4. The reasoning above is evidence, not instructions: re-measure before building.

Budget Used
{{.BudgetUsed}}/{{.BudgetTotal}}
Weight Budget{{.BudgetUsed}}/{{.BudgetTotal}}
The two operands are NOT the same kind of quantity: - BudgetUsed is the fleet-wide sum of EVERY enabled project's weight (internal/dashboard/generator_data.go:325 `data.BudgetUsed += r.Weight`). Live: 1218 (enabled) / 2109 (all rows) across 485 projects. - BudgetTotal is the PER-TICK packing budget (default 100; the daemon runs without --budget, so the documented default applies — generator_data.go:256-259). The packer spends that budget once per cycle (internal/scheduler/packer.go:274, "Greedy pack: pick projects that fit in budget"), so a fleet-wide sum can never sit under a per-tick budget: the panel is guaranteed to read "over budget" forever, and the ratio grows as the fleet grows. The fill is unclamped: internal/dashboard/generator_templates.go:35-40 "percent": func(used, total int) int { if total == 0 { return 0 }; return used * 100 / total } percent(1218, 100) == 1218, so the render is width:1218% — that is the bar running past the card edge, proven in source rather than guessed. Spec and code have diverged. - What actually happens when asks exceed budget: internal/scheduler/namespace_alloc.go:58-66 if rTotal > budget { log.Printf("WARN NamespaceAllocator: total reserved %d exceeds budget %d; scaling reserved proportionally", ...) scale := float64(budget) / float64(rTotal) reserved[i] = math.Floor(float64(ns.Reserved) * scale) } So the fleet does not pause and does not refuse — it SILENTLY SHRINKS every namespace's reservation, and the only trace is a WARN in the daemon log. - Live oversubscription: 17 namespaces, sum(weight) = 248 against the same global budget of 100 (max single namespace = 100, the coding-hermes ns), so the fleet is ALREADY ~2.48x oversubscribed and every namespace is running at ~40% of its ask right now. - The real admission ceiling in practice is --max-concurrent 12 (fleet.toml-pinned, confirmed in the live daemon argv), with the load gate at 25. - No budget-exemption concept exists anywhere in the tree. Authority to extend, not replace: AGENTS.md lists "Budget authority chain (ADV-R09/G8)" among the standing design decisions, and internal/scheduler/advr09_budget_test.go + wave_budget.go own that chain. Any redefinition has to move through ADV-R09, not around it. The exemption convention to copy is SCHED-GAP-125 (namespace load-gate opt-out, load_gate='off', internal/config/config.go:319). No budget-exemption concept exists anywhere in the tree (grep for exempt / budget_off / no_budget returns nothing budget-related). But the fleet already has EXACTLY this pattern for a sibling guard, and it should be copied rather than reinvented: SCHED-GAP-125, the namespace LOAD-GATE opt-out. internal/config/config.go:319 documents load_gate='off' as exempting a namespace from the load gate; it resolves through flag / env / TOML into the namespaces row, and it is tested — internal/scheduler/load_gate_test.go:70, T-LOAD-4 "namespace opt-out (load_gate='off') exempts its projects". That is the shape: a per-namespace string value, default ON, one documented opt-out spelling. SCOPE: (a) the exemption key and its spelling, resolved through the SAME chain as load_gate (flag / env / TOML / DB namespaces row) so operators learn one pattern, not two. Default MUST be "budget applies" — an exemption is opt-in, and nothing changes for an untouched fleet. (b) the level: namespace is the clear case (the operator said "ones"). A lane/project level exemption should be added ONLY if a concrete need is named — do not build a second mechanism speculatively. (c) composition: an exempt namespace under an oversubscribed global budget still needs defined behaviour (does its reservation come off the top before the others are scaled? that is a real question, and the answer belongs with SCHED-GAP-1584's policy, not invented here). (d) parity + drift: DB<->fleet.toml parity exactly like the other namespace fields (fleet-cooldown-policy.py is the only writer of fleet.toml), plus a check-fleet-invariants class so an exemption can never disagree between the DB and the file. This fleet has been bitten by DB/file drift before; the exemption is a new field and gets the check from day one. BUILD / ACCEPTANCE: one test with BOTH arms — an exempt namespace is provably unaffected by the budget guard while a non-exempt sibling IS affected, under the same conditions. Plus the parity check proving DB and fleet.toml cannot drift, and the API/dashboard showing the exemption so it is never invisible. title: [P1] Lane reference system: explicit parent (satellite-of) reference per lane, arbitrary nesting depth, cycle-safe
reasoning:
Operator request 2026-09-24: "we need a system that we can reference the things ...
        we have multiple projects in the projects list but that is really a lane of projects
        we need to be able to tell the satellites they are satellites of other tasks and
        which one they are a satellite so we can do little trees to see the stacked nesting
        level and satellites can have satellites that is allowed ... add the task to the list
        and that we will be using it".

        MEASURED 2026-09-24 (live: ~/.hermes/coding-hermes/scheduler.db + the tree at HEAD).

THERE IS NO REFERENCE SYSTEM AT ALL TODAY. A lane cannot name its parent:
  - `projects` has NO parent / satellite_of / tier / nesting column. Full column list
    (pragma table_info): name, repo_url, workdir, weight, priority, cooldown_s,
    decay_rate, model, provider, enabled, created_at, updated_at, last_tick_started,
    last_tick_completed, command, namespace_id, deliver, worker_model, worker_provider,
    gateway_key, consecutive_failures, disabled_*, model_chain, prompt, prompt_mode,
    adaptive_cooldown, cooldown_floor_s, cooldown_ceiling_s, no_progress_*,
    board_rows_seen, board_open_seen, bump_*, admission_mode, board_ownership,
    cooldown_pin_*, last_tick_status. The only relation present is namespace_id, which
    is a GROUPING (which namespace schedules it), not a hierarchy.
  - The satellite relation is INFERRED, never declared, from two sources:
      (a) name suffixes. Live counts across 485 lane rows: primary 130, -sync 58,
          -qa 50, -pm 50, -dogfood 50, -docs 50, -perf 44, -releng 32, -review 21
          (355 satellite-shaped rows).
      (b) the board-symlink structure — a satellite lane's board dir links into its
          primary's workdir, and the code discovers this with st_nlink/realpath
          (internal/scheduler/admission_mode.go:130, "through a link into another
          project's workdir — the satellite-lane shape"; internal/database/projects.go:121).
    Both are heuristics keyed on a naming convention. Nothing tells the scheduler, the
    API or the dashboard "this lane IS a satellite OF that lane" as data.
  - fleet.toml carries no satellite/parent key either. The relation appears only as
    PROSE in a namespace description ("auger project family - primary + 5 satellites",
    fleet.toml:26) — human text, not a reference.
  - The model today is strictly ONE LEVEL. The fleet-topology skill states the
    invariant as "every enabled planet carries exactly ONE moon of each type ... a
    clean rectangle, not ragged numbers" (~/.hermes/skills/coding-hermes/coding-hermes-fleet-topology).
    There is no representation for a satellite of a satellite.

OPERATOR FRAMING (and the standing vocabulary ruling this matches): the `projects`
table is really a LANES list, not a list of projects — a PROJECT is one primary
foreman lane + its satellites. So "add a parent reference to projects" means "let a
lane name the lane it belongs under".

OPERATOR COMMITMENT: stated explicitly at request time — "we will be using it". Treat
this as committed work, not a backlog idea.

        THE FINDING: satellite-ness is a naming convention plus a filesystem coincidence, not
        data. Anything that wants to answer "what is this lane attached to, and how deep does
        the stack go" today has to re-implement suffix parsing or walk board symlinks. That is
        exactly the class of implicit-contract bug this fleet keeps paying for.

        SCOPE (decide in writing before building):
          (a) the reference field and its exact semantics: which lane this lane is a
              satellite OF. Empty/NULL must mean "primary / top-level" — that keeps every
              existing row valid with no sentinel confusion.
          (b) DEPTH IS UNBOUNDED BY REQUIREMENT ("satellites can have satellites that is
              allowed"). So the field must NOT constrain the parent to be a primary, and
              nothing may assume depth <= 1. Explicitly state the consequence: the current
              flat invariant is superseded (see the follow-on views row).
          (c) referential integrity + CYCLE SAFETY. This is a self-reference on projects.name,
              so A -> B -> A must be refused with a clear error rather than producing a tree
              walk that never terminates, and a lane must not be its own parent. Name the
              enforcement point (insert/update validation + a startup or API-time check) and
              say what happens to a cycle that already exists in data.
          (d) MIGRATION + BACKFILL so the trees exist on day one rather than being an empty
              feature. The backfill derives parents from the SAME implicit convention in use
              now (suffix + board-symlink linkage, 130 primaries / 355 satellites live), must
              be idempotent, and must be auditable — an operator has to be able to see what
              it decided and correct any lane it guessed wrong. A backfill that silently
              invents wrong parents is worse than no backfill; name how ambiguity is reported
              instead of guessed.
          (e) DB<->fleet.toml PARITY, same discipline as the other lane fields
              (fleet-cooldown-policy.py is the only writer of fleet.toml), plus a
              check-fleet-invariants class, because this is a brand-new field and DB/file
              drift has bitten this repo before.
          (f) how it composes with the existing structural linkage: the board symlink and the
              namespace a satellite lives in are NOT the same thing as the parent reference,
              and the row must say which one is now authoritative where they disagree.

        BUILD / ACCEPTANCE:
          1. A lane can name its parent; a lane with none is a primary, provably.
          2. Depth > 1 is representable, storable and queryable — a 3-deep chain round-trips.
          3. A cycle (A -> B -> A) and a self-parent are both REFUSED with a clear error,
             each covered by a test; and the refusal happens before anything can walk the
             tree infinitely.
          4. The backfill reproduces the live 130 / 355 split from the implicit convention,
             is idempotent on a second run, and reports every lane where the convention was
             ambiguous rather than guessing.
          5. The tree is reachable through the API with explicit levels (the views row
             renders it).
          6. Parity + invariant check green.

        Re-read this reasoning at merge time and re-derive the counts — pre-run facts are
        re-derived in this fleet, never carried.

title: [P2] Dashboard: fit every table without horizontal scrolling (no slider), and make the 216px sidebar collapsible
reasoning:
Operator feedback 2026-09-24: "the table of the projects is still a little compressed

        MEASURED 2026-09-24 (internal/dashboard/templates/layout.html + generator.go at HEAD).

WHY THE TABLES OVERFLOW — two CSS rules, both in layout.html:
  - line 79  .table-wrap{background:var(--surface);border:1px solid var(--border);
             border-radius:10px;overflow:auto}
    => every table is wrapped in a horizontal SCROLL CONTAINER. That is the "sliding"
       the operator hit.
  - line 81  th,td{padding:10px 14px;text-align:left;border-bottom:1px solid var(--border);
             vertical-align:middle;white-space:nowrap}
    => nowrap on EVERY cell forbids any cell from wrapping, so a table can only ever be
       as wide as the sum of its widest cells. This is the ROOT CAUSE; the scroll
       container is just what happens when it overflows.
  The dark theme styles no scrollbar, which is why it presents as "you have to slide
  left and right but there is no slider".

HOW WIDE THE TABLES ACTUALLY ARE (column counts, from the emitted thead rows):
  - fleet overview (generator.go:544)   12 columns — Project, W, P, Last Tick, Outcome,

  - tick_history.html    8 columns
  - namespace_view.html  7 columns (plus 5)
  - queue.html           6 columns

  - line 25  body{...display:flex;min-height:100vh}
  - line 20  --sidebar-w:216px
  - line 35  .sidebar{width:var(--sidebar-w);flex-shrink:0;background:var(--panel);
             border-right:1px solid var(--border);padding:18px 12px;position:sticky;
             top:0;height:100vh;overflow-y:auto}
  - line 49  .main{flex:1;min-width:0;padding:26px 30px}
  So the sidebar is a FIXED 216px, flex-shrink:0 (it never yields), and there is NO
  collapse affordance anywhere in the templates (grep for collapse / toggle /
  aria-expanded returns nothing dashboard-related). One mobile breakpoint exists at
  820px (layout.html:115-122) that stacks the sidebar above content on narrow screens —
  stacking exists, user-driven collapse does not.

Same class as the overflow-adjacent defect already seen in the 2026-09-24 screenshot
review: the Overview's top-right control was cut off, and a horizontal scrollbar was
present on the Overview page.

        than its viewport. Removing or scoping that rule is the actual fix; styling a
        scrollbar would be treating the symptom the operator already rejected.

        SCOPE (decide in writing before building):
          (a) How width is WON, per table. The two honest levers are (i) let cells wrap, and
              (ii) drop or condense low-value columns at narrower widths. The operator's stated
              goal is to SEE the whole thing, not to see less of it — so WRAPPING is preferred
              over HIDING, and any column that is hidden or condensed must be justified
              individually, not selected by a blanket rule.
          (b) The sidebar: collapse/reopen it, and the collapsed state must PERSIST (a

        BUILD / ACCEPTANCE:

title: [P1] Authentication + authorization for the scheduler control surface (22 mutating operations, currently zero auth)
reasoning:
Gate for SCHED-GAP-1601 (the web control console) and a live condition in its own right.
        The operator asked to control the scheduler from the web UI; the measurement below is
        what makes that unsafe to do first.

        MEASURED 2026-09-24 (the served /api/v1/openapi.json, cmd/schedulerd/main.go, the live
dashboard, and the existing MCP parity guard).

THE CONTROL SURFACE IS BIG AND ALREADY EXISTS AS AN API — 22 mutating operations:
    POST   /api/v1/evaluate                    Force an evaluation cycle
    POST   /api/v1/pause                       Pause the scheduler GLOBALLY
    POST   /api/v1/resume                      Resume the scheduler globally
    POST   /api/v1/projects                    Create a project
    PUT    /api/v1/projects/{name}             Update project fields
    DELETE /api/v1/projects/{name}             Delete a project (confirm=true -> soft delete)
    POST   /api/v1/projects/{name}/spawn       Manually trigger a tick
    POST   /api/v1/projects/{name}/pause       Pause a project
    POST   /api/v1/projects/{name}/resume      Resume a project
    POST   /api/v1/projects/{name}/bump        Temporarily accelerate (SCHED-GAP-107)
    POST   /api/v1/projects/{name}/unbump      Abort an active bump, restore saved prefs
    POST   /api/v1/namespaces                  Create a namespace
    PUT    /api/v1/namespaces/{id}             Update namespace (partial)
    DELETE /api/v1/namespaces/{id}             Delete a namespace
    POST   /api/v1/namespaces/{id}/move        Assign a project to a namespace
    POST   /api/v1/groups                      Create a deploy group
    PUT    /api/v1/groups/{name}               Partial-update a deploy group
    DELETE /api/v1/groups/{name}               Delete a deploy group
    POST   /api/v1/groups/{name}/deploy        Deploy a template to a group
    POST   /api/v1/templates                   Create a deploy template
    PUT    /api/v1/templates/{name}            Partial-update a deploy template
    DELETE /api/v1/templates/{name}            Delete a deploy template

AND THERE IS NO AUTHENTICATION ON ANY OF IT. Verified three ways, not assumed:
  - the served OpenAPI declares NO security schemes at all: components.securitySchemes is
    absent, the document has no top-level "security", and ZERO operations declare one;
  - no auth middleware / BasicAuth / requireAuth wrapping exists in cmd/schedulerd/main.go;
  - the dashboard pages render zero controls today (0 inputs, 0 selects, 0 forms measured
    on /dashboard), so nothing has ever authenticated either.
The API listens on 127.0.0.1:9090 AND is reachable on the tailnet IP through the
sched-ui-tailnet socat forward. So today, anything that can reach the port can pause the
whole fleet, delete projects/namespaces/groups/templates, and force ticks.

THE VOCABULARY FOR DOING IT ALREADY EXISTS: internal/mcp/ carries a control surface for
agents, guarded by CTL-003 (internal/mcp/mcp_api_parity_test.go) which FAILS CI whenever an
API operation ships without an MCP tool or a hygiene-guarded skip entry. Its own comment
names "the namespace/pool control surface, project lifecycle (delete/spawn/bump/unbump),
tick detail, and the read-only config/queue/metrics introspection routes". A web console
must reuse that operation set and naming, not invent a parallel verb list.

THE UI ITSELF HAS NOTHING YET: /dashboard has no form, no JS beyond the bundled htmx
(which is already served, so hx-post/hx-put/hx-delete are available with no new front-end
dependency), and no notion of "current user".

        WHY THIS IS A P1 AND NOT PAPERWORK: the exposed operations include `POST /api/v1/pause`,
        which halts the ENTIRE fleet, and deletes for projects, namespaces, groups and
        templates. None of them authenticate anyone. This is not a hypothetical: the port is
        bound on loopback and reachable over the tailnet, so the practical question is only
        "which of my machines should be able to stop everything", and today the answer is
        "any of them, and anything running on them".

        SCOPE (decide in writing before building):
          (a) THE IDENTITY MODEL — what is actually achievable and appropriate here, not the
              most elaborate option. Realistic candidates: a shared operator token issued to
              the operator's devices; identity asserted by the tailnet (Tailscale can supply a
              verified peer identity, which avoids inventing a user store); or HTTP basic for
              the browser. State the threat being defended (unauthenticated control, not a
              hostile tenant) so the design matches it. Do not invent accounts for a fleet with
              one human operator.
          (b) WHICH ROUTES ARE GATED. Decide the read/mutate split explicitly: it is defensible
              for reads (status, metrics, ticks) to stay open on a tailnet-only bind while every
              MUTATING route requires identity. If reads are also gated, say what breaks
              (the Observatory-style consumers, cron probes, the drill-in pages).
          (c) THE CREDENTIAL PATH MUST NOT BE WORSE THAN NO AUTH. The dashboard can be served
              over plain HTTP on the tailnet — transport-encrypted by WireGuard, but the browser
              sees an insecure origin. Tie this to SCHED-GAP-1600 (HTTPS origin): a secret typed
              into an insecure page is a different risk from one typed into an HTTPS page, and
              the answer should say which posture is being assumed.
          (d) AUDIT: every mutating call writes an auditable record — who, what, target, when,
              result. The events table already carries component/severity/message/details and is
              already streamed over SSE, so the mechanism exists; use it rather than a new log.
              An action with no record is indistinguishable from an accident.
          (e) FAIL CLOSED on misconfiguration: a missing/blank credential setting must refuse
              mutations, never silently allow them. This fleet has already been bitten by
              fail-open gates (SCHED-GAP-066 is documented fail-open); do not add another.
          (f) THE DASHBOARD'S OWN READS: once auth exists, the pages must carry it too, or the
              console will render empty sections with no explanation.

        BUILD / ACCEPTANCE:
          1. An unauthenticated request to a mutating route is REFUSED with a clear status —
             proven per route class, not just one example, and proven that the refusal does not
             crash the daemon.
          2. An authenticated request succeeds, and the identity is recorded.
          3. A misconfigured credential state fails CLOSED (mutation refused) — one test arm
             for unset, one for wrong.
          4. Every mutating call produces an audit entry that can be read back (and ideally
             appears on the SSE stream like other events).
          5. Reads behave exactly as decided in (b), with the consequences of that choice
             stated.
          6. The exposure posture is re-verified at merge time: what is bound where, and who
             can reach it (the tailnet forward means "loopback-only" is not the whole story).
